title: “It’s Mother!”
paragraphs: The children’s faith in the Magic never wavered. After the morning chants, Colin sometimes gave them a lecture on it.

“I like doing this,” he explained, “because when I grow up and make great scientific discoveries, I’ll have to lecture about them, so this is practice. I can only give short lectures now, because I’m very young. Besides, Ben Weatherstaff would feel like he was in church and fall asleep.”
“The best thing about lecturing,” said Ben, “is that a fellow can stand up and say whatever he likes, and no other fellow can talk back. I wouldn’t mind doing a bit of lecturing myself sometimes.”

But whenever Colin spoke from under his tree, old Ben stared at him hungrily and never looked away. He studied the boy with a critical sort of fondness. It was not really the lecture that interested him. It was the legs that looked straighter and stronger every day, the head that held itself so well, the sharp chin and hollow cheeks that had filled out and rounded, and the eyes that were starting to shine with a light he remembered seeing in another pair. Sometimes Colin took Ben’s earnest gaze to mean he was deeply impressed, and he wondered what the old man was thinking. Once, when Ben seemed completely spellbound, Colin asked him.
“What are you thinking about, Ben Weatherstaff?” he asked.
“I was thinking,” answered Ben, “that I’d bet you’ve put on three or four pounds this week. I was looking at your calves and your shoulders. I’d like to get you on a pair of scales.”
“It’s the Magic, and—and Mrs. Sowerby’s buns and milk and things,” said Colin. “You see, the scientific experiment has worked.”

That morning Dickon was too late to hear the lecture. When he arrived, he was red-faced from running, and his funny face looked even more twinkling than usual. There was a lot of weeding to do after the rains, so they got right to work. There was always plenty to do after a warm, soaking rain. The wet that was so good for the flowers was just as good for the weeds, which pushed up tiny blades of grass and little points of leaves. These had to be pulled out before their roots took too firm a hold. Colin was as good at weeding as anyone by now, and he could lecture while he did it.

“The Magic works best when you work too,” he said this morning. “You can feel it in your bones and muscles. I’m going to read books about bones and muscles, but I’m going to write a book about Magic. I’m making it up now. I keep discovering new things.”

Not long after he said this, he put down his trowel and stood up. He had been quiet for several minutes, and they could tell he was thinking up lectures, as he often did. When he dropped his trowel and stood up straight, it seemed to Mary and Dickon that a sudden, powerful thought had made him do it. He stretched himself to his full height and flung his arms out joyfully. Color glowed in his face, and his strange eyes opened wide with happiness. All at once he had understood something completely.
“Mary! Dickon!” he cried. “Just look at me!”
They stopped weeding and looked at him.
“Do you remember that first morning you brought me in here?” he demanded.
Dickon was looking at him very hard. Because he was an animal charmer, he could see more than most people could, and much of what he saw he never talked about. He saw some of it now in this boy.
“Aye, we do,” he answered.
Mary looked hard too, but she said nothing.
“Just this minute,” said Colin, “it all came back to me—when I looked at my hand digging with the trowel—and I had to stand up to see if it was real. And it is real! I’m _well_—I’m _well!_”
“Aye, that you are!” said Dickon.
“I’m well! I’m well!” said Colin again, and his whole face turned red.

In a way he had known it before. He had hoped it, felt it and thought about it. But at that very moment something had rushed through him, a kind of rapturous belief and understanding. It was so strong that he could not help crying out.

“I’ll live forever and ever and ever!” he cried grandly. “I’ll find out thousands and thousands of things. I’ll learn about people and animals and everything that grows—like Dickon—and I’ll never stop making Magic. I’m well! I’m well! I feel—I feel as if I want to shout something—something grateful and joyful!”
Ben Weatherstaff, who had been working near a rose bush, glanced around at him.
“You could sing the Doxology,” he suggested in his driest grunt. He had no great opinion of the Doxology, and he did not offer the idea with any special respect.
But Colin had an exploring mind, and he knew nothing about the Doxology.
“What is that?” he asked.
“Dickon can sing it for you, I’ll bet,” replied Ben Weatherstaff.
Dickon answered with his smile that saw everything, the smile of an animal charmer.
“They sing it in church,” he said. “Mother says she believes the skylarks sing it when they get up in the morning.”
“If your mother says so, it must be a lovely song,” Colin replied. “I’ve never set foot in a church. I was always too sick to go. Please sing it, Dickon. I’d like to hear it.”

Dickon was simple and natural about it. He understood what Colin was feeling better than Colin did himself. He understood it by a kind of instinct so natural that he did not know it was understanding. He pulled off his cap and looked around, still smiling.
“You must take off your cap,” he said to Colin, “and so must you, Ben—and you must stand up, you know.”

Colin took off his cap, and the sun shone on his thick hair and warmed it while he watched Dickon closely. Ben Weatherstaff scrambled up from his knees and bared his head too. He had a puzzled, half-resentful look on his old face, as if he didn’t quite know why he was doing this remarkable thing.
Dickon stood among the trees and rose bushes and began to sing, in a plain, matter-of-fact way and with a fine, strong boy’s voice:

“Praise God from whom all blessings flow,
Praise Him all creatures here below,
Praise Him above, you Heavenly Host,
Praise Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.
Amen.”
When he finished, Ben Weatherstaff was standing perfectly still, his jaw set stubbornly, but with a troubled look in his eyes as he stared at Colin. Colin’s face was thoughtful and grateful.

“It is a very nice song,” he said. “I like it. Maybe it means just what I mean when I want to shout that I’m thankful to the Magic.” He stopped and thought, puzzled. “Maybe they’re both the same thing. How can we know the exact names of everything? Sing it again, Dickon. Let’s try, Mary. I want to sing it too. It’s my song. How does it begin? ‘Praise God from whom all blessings flow’?”

And they sang it again. Mary and Colin raised their voices as musically as they could, and Dickon’s swelled out loud and beautiful. At the second line Ben Weatherstaff cleared his throat with a rasp, and at the third line he joined in so vigorously that it sounded almost wild. When the “Amen” ended, Mary saw that the same thing had happened to him that had happened when he found out Colin was not a cripple. His chin was twitching, he was staring and blinking, and his leathery old cheeks were wet.
“I never saw any sense in the Doxology before,” he said hoarsely, “but I may change my mind in time. I’d say you’ve put on five pounds this week, Master Colin—five of them!”
Colin was looking across the garden at something that had caught his attention, and his face had turned startled.
“Who is coming in here?” he said quickly. “Who is it?”

The door in the ivy-covered wall had been pushed gently open, and a woman had come in. She had entered with the last line of their song and had stood still, listening and looking at them. The ivy was behind her, sunlight drifted through the trees and dappled her long blue cloak, and her fresh, kind face was smiling across the greenery. She looked like a softly colored picture in one of Colin’s books. She had wonderful, loving eyes that seemed to take everything in—all of them, even Ben Weatherstaff and the “creatures” and every flower in bloom. Although she had appeared so suddenly, not one of them felt that she was an intruder at all. Dickon’s eyes lit up like lamps.
“It’s Mother—that’s who it is!” he cried, and he ran across the grass.
Colin started toward her too, and Mary went with him. Both of them felt their hearts beat faster.
“It’s Mother!” Dickon said again when they met halfway. “I knew you wanted to see her, and I told her where the door was hidden.”
Colin held out his hand with a flushed, royal sort of shyness, but his eyes drank in her face.
“Even back when I was sick, I wanted to meet you,” he said, “you and Dickon and the secret garden. Before that, I had never wanted to see anybody or anything at all.”
The sight of his lifted face brought a sudden change over hers. She flushed, the corners of her mouth trembled, and a mist seemed to pass over her eyes.

“Eh! Dear lad!” she burst out, trembling. “Eh! Dear lad!” She said it as if she had not known she was going to. She did not say “Master Colin,” but just “dear lad,” quite suddenly. She might have said it to Dickon in the same way if she had seen something in his face that touched her. Colin liked it.
“Are you surprised because I’m so well?” he asked.
She put her hand on his shoulder and smiled the mist out of her eyes.
“Aye, I am!” she said. “But you’re so like your mother that you made my heart jump.”
“Do you think,” said Colin, a little awkwardly, “that it will make my father like me?”
“Aye, for sure, dear lad,” she answered, and she gave his shoulder a soft, quick pat. “He must come home—he must come home.”

“Susan Sowerby,” said Ben Weatherstaff, stepping close to her. “Look at the lad’s legs, will you? They were like drumsticks in stockings two months ago—and I heard folks say they were bandy and knock-kneed both at the same time. Look at them now!”
Susan Sowerby gave a comfortable laugh.

“They’re going to be fine strong lad’s legs before long,” she said. “Let him keep on playing and working in the garden and eating heartily and drinking plenty of good sweet milk, and there’ll not be a finer pair in Yorkshire, thank God for it.”
She put both hands on Mistress Mary’s shoulders and looked over her small face the way a mother would.

“And you too!” she said. “You’ve grown nearly as hearty as our ’Lisabeth Ellen. I’ll bet you’re like your mother too. Our Martha told me Mrs. Medlock had heard she was a pretty woman. You’ll be like a blush rose when you grow up, my little lass, bless you.”

She did not mention that when Martha came home on her “day out” and described the plain, sallow child, she had said she had no confidence at all in what Mrs. Medlock had heard. “It doesn’t stand to reason that a pretty woman could be the mother of such a plain little lass,” she had added stubbornly.

Mary had not had time to pay much attention to how her face was changing. She had only noticed that she looked “different,” that she seemed to have a great deal more hair, and that it was growing very fast. But she remembered how much she had enjoyed looking at the Mem Sahib in the past, so she was glad to hear she might one day look like her.

Susan Sowerby walked around their garden with them, heard the whole story of it, and was shown every bush and tree that had come alive. Colin walked on one side of her and Mary on the other. They kept looking up at her comfortable, rosy face, secretly curious about the lovely feeling she gave them, a warm, supported sort of feeling. It seemed that she understood them the way Dickon understood his “creatures.” She bent over the flowers and talked about them as if they were children. Soot followed her, cawed at her once or twice, and flew onto her shoulder as if it were Dickon’s. When they told her about the robin and the first flight of the young ones, she gave a mellow, motherly little laugh deep in her throat.
“I suppose teaching them to fly is like teaching children to walk, but I’m afraid I’d be in a terrible worry if mine had wings instead of legs,” she said.
She seemed such a wonderful woman, in her kind moorland cottage way, that at last they told her about the Magic.
“Do you believe in Magic?” asked Colin, after he had explained about Indian fakirs. “I do hope you do.”

“I do, lad,” she answered. “I never knew it by that name, but what does the name matter? I’d bet they call it something different in France and something different again in Germany. The same thing that set the seeds swelling and the sun shining made you a well lad, and it’s the Good Thing. It isn’t like us poor fools, who think it matters if we’re called by the wrong name. The Big Good Thing doesn’t stop to worry, bless you. It goes on making worlds by the million—worlds like ours. Never stop believing in the Big Good Thing and knowing the world is full of it—and call it whatever you like. You were singing to it when I came into the garden.”

“I was so happy,” said Colin, gazing at her with his beautiful, strange eyes. “All at once I noticed how different I was—how strong my arms and legs had become, you see—and how I could dig and stand—so I leaped up and wanted to shout something to whatever would hear me.”

“The Magic listened when you sang the Doxology. It would have listened to anything you sang. It was the joy that mattered. Eh! Lad, lad—what are names to the Joy Maker?” And she gave his shoulders a quick, soft pat again.

She had packed a basket that held a real feast this morning. When the hungry hour came and Dickon brought it out from its hiding place, she sat down with them under their tree and watched them gobble up their food, laughing and delighting in their appetites. She was full of fun and made them laugh at all sorts of silly things. She told them stories in broad Yorkshire and taught them new words. She laughed as if she couldn’t help it when they told her how hard it was getting to pretend that Colin was still a fretful invalid.

“You see, we can’t help laughing nearly all the time when we’re together,” explained Colin. “And it doesn’t sound sick at all. We try to choke it back, but it bursts out, and that sounds worse than ever.”

“There’s one thing that comes into my mind so often,” said Mary, “and I can hardly ever hold in my laughter when I suddenly think of it. I keep thinking, what if Colin’s face starts to look like a full moon? It isn’t like one yet, but he gets a tiny bit fatter every day—and what if one morning it looks like one—what would we do!”
“Bless us all, I can see you’ve a good bit of play-acting to do,” said Susan Sowerby. “But you won’t have to keep it up much longer. Master Craven will come home.”
“Do you think he will?” asked Colin. “Why?”
Susan Sowerby chuckled softly.
“I suppose it would nearly break your heart if he found out before you told him in your own way,” she said. “You’ve lain awake nights planning it.”
“I couldn’t stand it if somebody else told him,” said Colin. “Every day I think of a new way to do it. Today I think I’d like to simply run straight into his room.”
“That would be a fine surprise for him,” said Susan Sowerby. “I’d like to see his face, lad. I would indeed! He must come back—he must.”

One of the things they talked about was the visit they would make to her cottage. They planned it all out. They would drive over the moor and eat lunch outdoors among the heather. They would see all twelve children and Dickon’s garden, and they would not come back until they were tired.

At last Susan Sowerby got up to go back to the house and Mrs. Medlock. It was time for Colin to be wheeled back as well. But before he got into his chair, he stood very close to Susan and fixed his eyes on her with a kind of bewildered adoration. Suddenly he caught hold of a fold of her blue cloak and held on tight.
“You are just what I—what I wanted,” he said. “I wish you were my mother—as well as Dickon’s!”

All at once Susan Sowerby bent down and pulled him close, wrapping her warm arms around him against her chest under the blue cloak, as if he were Dickon’s own brother. A quick mist came over her eyes.
“Eh! Dear lad!” she said. “Your own mother is in this very garden, I do believe. She couldn’t keep out of it. Your father must come back to you—he must!”
